# regex_lite/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)This crate provides a **lightweight** regex engine for searching strings. The
[3](https://docs.rs#3)regex syntax supported by this crate is nearly identical to what is found in
[4](https://docs.rs#4)the [`regex`](https://docs.rs/regex) crate. Like the `regex` crate, all regex
[5](https://docs.rs#5)searches in this crate have worst case `O(m * n)` time complexity, where `m` is
[6](https://docs.rs#6)proportional to the size of the regex and `n` is proportional to the size of
[7](https://docs.rs#7)the string being searched.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)The principal difference between the `regex` and `regex-lite` crates is that
[10](https://docs.rs#10)the latter prioritizes smaller binary sizes and shorter Rust compile times
[11](https://docs.rs#11)over performance and functionality. As a result, regex searches in this crate
[12](https://docs.rs#12)are typically substantially slower than what is provided by the `regex` crate.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)Moreover, this crate only has the most basic level of Unicode support: it
[14](https://docs.rs#14)matches codepoint by codepoint but otherwise doesn't support Unicode case
[15](https://docs.rs#15)insensitivity or things like `\p{Letter}`. In exchange, this crate contributes
[16](https://docs.rs#16)far less to binary size and compiles much more quickly.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)If you just want API documentation, then skip to the [`Regex`] type. Otherwise,
[19](https://docs.rs#19)here's a quick example showing one way of parsing the output of a grep-like
[20](https://docs.rs#20)program:
[21](https://docs.rs#21)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)```rust
[23](https://docs.rs#23)use regex_lite::Regex;
[24](https://docs.rs#24)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^([^:]+):([0-9]+):(.+)$").unwrap();
[26](https://docs.rs#26)let hay = "\
[27](https://docs.rs#27)path/to/foo:54:Blue Harvest
[28](https://docs.rs#28)path/to/bar:90:Something, Something, Something, Dark Side
[29](https://docs.rs#29)path/to/baz:3:It's a Trap!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)";
[31](https://docs.rs#31)
[32](https://docs.rs#32)let mut results = vec![];
[33](https://docs.rs#33)for (_, [path, lineno, line]) in re.captures_iter(hay).map(|c| c.extract()) {
[34](https://docs.rs#34)    results.push((path, lineno.parse::<u64>()?, line));
[35](https://docs.rs#35)}
[36](https://docs.rs#36)assert_eq!(results, vec![
[37](https://docs.rs#37)    ("path/to/foo", 54, "Blue Harvest"),
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    ("path/to/bar", 90, "Something, Something, Something, Dark Side"),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    ("path/to/baz", 3, "It's a Trap!"),
[40](https://docs.rs#40)]);
[41](https://docs.rs#41)# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
[42](https://docs.rs#42)```
[43](https://docs.rs#43)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)# Overview
[45](https://docs.rs#45)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)The primary type in this crate is a [`Regex`]. Its most important methods are
[47](https://docs.rs#47)as follows:
[48](https://docs.rs#48)
[49](https://docs.rs#49)* [`Regex::new`] compiles a regex using the default configuration. A
[50](https://docs.rs#50)[`RegexBuilder`] permits setting a non-default configuration. (For example,
[51](https://docs.rs#51)case insensitive matching, verbose mode and others.)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)* [`Regex::is_match`] reports whether a match exists in a particular haystack.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)* [`Regex::find`] reports the byte offsets of a match in a haystack, if one
[54](https://docs.rs#54)exists. [`Regex::find_iter`] returns an iterator over all such matches.
[55](https://docs.rs#55)* [`Regex::captures`] returns a [`Captures`], which reports both the byte
[56](https://docs.rs#56)offsets of a match in a haystack and the byte offsets of each matching capture
[57](https://docs.rs#57)group from the regex in the haystack.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)[`Regex::captures_iter`] returns an iterator over all such matches.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)
[60](https://docs.rs#60)Otherwise, this top-level crate documentation is organized as follows:
[61](https://docs.rs#61)
[62](https://docs.rs#62)* [Usage](#usage) shows how to add the `regex` crate to your Rust project.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)* [Examples](#examples) provides a limited selection of regex search examples.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)* [Differences with the regex crate](#differences-with-the-regex-crate)
[65](https://docs.rs#65)provides a precise description of how `regex-lite` differs from `regex`.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)* [Syntax](#syntax) enumerates the specific regex syntax supported by this
[67](https://docs.rs#67)crate.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)* [Untrusted input](#untrusted-input) discusses how this crate deals with regex
[69](https://docs.rs#69)patterns or haystacks that are untrusted.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)
[71](https://docs.rs#71)# Usage
[72](https://docs.rs#72)
[73](https://docs.rs#73)The `regex-lite` crate is [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/regex-lite)
[74](https://docs.rs#74)and can be used by adding `regex-lite` to your dependencies in your project's
[75](https://docs.rs#75)`Cargo.toml`. Or more simply, just run `cargo add regex-lite`.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)
[77](https://docs.rs#77)Here is a complete example that creates a new Rust project, adds a dependency
[78](https://docs.rs#78)on `regex-lite`, creates the source code for a regex search and then runs the
[79](https://docs.rs#79)program.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)
[81](https://docs.rs#81)First, create the project in a new directory:
[82](https://docs.rs#82)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)```text
[84](https://docs.rs#84)$ mkdir regex-example
[85](https://docs.rs#85)$ cd regex-example
[86](https://docs.rs#86)$ cargo init
[87](https://docs.rs#87)```
[88](https://docs.rs#88)
[89](https://docs.rs#89)Second, add a dependency on `regex`:
[90](https://docs.rs#90)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)```text
[92](https://docs.rs#92)$ cargo add regex-lite
[93](https://docs.rs#93)```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)
[95](https://docs.rs#95)Third, edit `src/main.rs`. Delete what's there and replace it with this:
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)```
[98](https://docs.rs#98)use regex_lite::Regex;
[99](https://docs.rs#99)
[100](https://docs.rs#100)fn main() {
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    let re = Regex::new(r"Hello (?<name>\w+)!").unwrap();
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    let Some(caps) = re.captures("Hello Murphy!") else {
[103](https://docs.rs#103)        println!("no match!");
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        return;
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    };
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    println!("The name is: {}", &caps["name"]);
[107](https://docs.rs#107)}
[108](https://docs.rs#108)```
[109](https://docs.rs#109)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)Fourth, run it with `cargo run`:
[111](https://docs.rs#111)
[112](https://docs.rs#112)```text
[113](https://docs.rs#113)$ cargo run
[114](https://docs.rs#114)   Compiling regex-lite v0.1.0
[115](https://docs.rs#115)   Compiling regex-example v0.1.0 (/tmp/regex-example)
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 4.22s
[117](https://docs.rs#117)     Running `target/debug/regex-example`
[118](https://docs.rs#118)The name is: Murphy
[119](https://docs.rs#119)```
[120](https://docs.rs#120)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)The first time you run the program will show more output like above. But
[122](https://docs.rs#122)subsequent runs shouldn't have to re-compile the dependencies.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)# Examples
[125](https://docs.rs#125)
[126](https://docs.rs#126)This section provides a few examples, in tutorial style, showing how to
[127](https://docs.rs#127)search a haystack with a regex. There are more examples throughout the API
[128](https://docs.rs#128)documentation.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)
[130](https://docs.rs#130)Before starting though, it's worth defining a few terms:
[131](https://docs.rs#131)
[132](https://docs.rs#132)* A **regex** is a Rust value whose type is `Regex`. We use `re` as a
[133](https://docs.rs#133)variable name for a regex.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)* A **pattern** is the string that is used to build a regex. We use `pat` as
[135](https://docs.rs#135)a variable name for a pattern.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)* A **haystack** is the string that is searched by a regex. We use `hay` as a
[137](https://docs.rs#137)variable name for a haystack.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)Sometimes the words "regex" and "pattern" are used interchangeably.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)
[141](https://docs.rs#141)General use of regular expressions in this crate proceeds by compiling a
[142](https://docs.rs#142)**pattern** into a **regex**, and then using that regex to search, split or
[143](https://docs.rs#143)replace parts of a **haystack**.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)### Example: find a middle initial
[146](https://docs.rs#146)
[147](https://docs.rs#147)We'll start off with a very simple example: a regex that looks for a specific
[148](https://docs.rs#148)name but uses a wildcard to match a middle initial. Our pattern serves as
[149](https://docs.rs#149)something like a template that will match a particular name with *any* middle
[150](https://docs.rs#150)initial.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)```rust
[153](https://docs.rs#153)use regex_lite::Regex;
[154](https://docs.rs#154)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)// We use 'unwrap()' here because it would be a bug in our program if the
[156](https://docs.rs#156)// pattern failed to compile to a regex. Panicking in the presence of a bug
[157](https://docs.rs#157)// is okay.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)let re = Regex::new(r"Homer (.)\. Simpson").unwrap();
[159](https://docs.rs#159)let hay = "Homer J. Simpson";
[160](https://docs.rs#160)let Some(caps) = re.captures(hay) else { return };
[161](https://docs.rs#161)assert_eq!("J", &caps[1]);
[162](https://docs.rs#162)```
[163](https://docs.rs#163)
[164](https://docs.rs#164)There are a few things worth noticing here in our first example:
[165](https://docs.rs#165)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)* The `.` is a special pattern meta character that means "match any single
[167](https://docs.rs#167)character except for new lines." (More precisely, in this crate, it means
[168](https://docs.rs#168)"match any UTF-8 encoding of any Unicode scalar value other than `\n`.")
[169](https://docs.rs#169)* We can match an actual `.` literally by escaping it, i.e., `\.`.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)* We use Rust's [raw strings] to avoid needing to deal with escape sequences in
[171](https://docs.rs#171)both the regex pattern syntax and in Rust's string literal syntax. If we didn't
[172](https://docs.rs#172)use raw strings here, we would have had to use `\\.` to match a literal `.`
[173](https://docs.rs#173)character. That is, `r"\."` and `"\\."` are equivalent patterns.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)* We put our wildcard `.` instruction in parentheses. These parentheses have a
[175](https://docs.rs#175)special meaning that says, "make whatever part of the haystack matches within
[176](https://docs.rs#176)these parentheses available as a capturing group." After finding a match, we
[177](https://docs.rs#177)access this capture group with `&caps[1]`.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)
[179](https://docs.rs#179)[raw strings]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)Otherwise, we execute a search using `re.captures(hay)` and return from our
[182](https://docs.rs#182)function if no match occurred. We then reference the middle initial by asking
[183](https://docs.rs#183)for the part of the haystack that matched the capture group indexed at `1`.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)(The capture group at index 0 is implicit and always corresponds to the entire
[185](https://docs.rs#185)match. In this case, that's `Homer J. Simpson`.)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)
[187](https://docs.rs#187)### Example: named capture groups
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)Continuing from our middle initial example above, we can tweak the pattern
[190](https://docs.rs#190)slightly to give a name to the group that matches the middle initial:
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)```rust
[193](https://docs.rs#193)use regex_lite::Regex;
[194](https://docs.rs#194)
[195](https://docs.rs#195)// Note that (?P<middle>.) is a different way to spell the same thing.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)let re = Regex::new(r"Homer (?<middle>.)\. Simpson").unwrap();
[197](https://docs.rs#197)let hay = "Homer J. Simpson";
[198](https://docs.rs#198)let Some(caps) = re.captures(hay) else { return };
[199](https://docs.rs#199)assert_eq!("J", &caps["middle"]);
[200](https://docs.rs#200)```
[201](https://docs.rs#201)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)Giving a name to a group can be useful when there are multiple groups in
[203](https://docs.rs#203)a pattern. It makes the code referring to those groups a bit easier to
[204](https://docs.rs#204)understand.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)### Example: validating a particular date format
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)This examples shows how to confirm whether a haystack, in its entirety, matches
[209](https://docs.rs#209)a particular date format:
[210](https://docs.rs#210)
[211](https://docs.rs#211)```rust
[212](https://docs.rs#212)use regex_lite::Regex;
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)let re = Regex::new(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$").unwrap();
[215](https://docs.rs#215)assert!(re.is_match("2010-03-14"));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)```
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)Notice the use of the `^` and `$` anchors. In this crate, every regex search is
[219](https://docs.rs#219)run with an implicit `(?s:.)*?` at the beginning of its pattern, which allows
[220](https://docs.rs#220)the regex to match anywhere in a haystack. Anchors, as above, can be used to
[221](https://docs.rs#221)ensure that the full haystack matches a pattern.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)### Example: finding dates in a haystack
[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)In the previous example, we showed how one might validate that a haystack,
[226](https://docs.rs#226)in its entirety, corresponded to a particular date format. But what if we wanted
[227](https://docs.rs#227)to extract all things that look like dates in a specific format from a haystack?
[228](https://docs.rs#228)To do this, we can use an iterator API to find all matches (notice that we've
[229](https://docs.rs#229)removed the anchors):
[230](https://docs.rs#230)
[231](https://docs.rs#231)```rust
[232](https://docs.rs#232)use regex_lite::Regex;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)let re = Regex::new(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}").unwrap();
[235](https://docs.rs#235)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[236](https://docs.rs#236)// 'm' is a 'Match', and 'as_str()' returns the matching part of the haystack.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)let dates: Vec<&str> = re.find_iter(hay).map(|m| m.as_str()).collect();
[238](https://docs.rs#238)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    "1865-04-14",
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    "1881-07-02",
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    "1901-09-06",
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    "1963-11-22",
[243](https://docs.rs#243)]);
[244](https://docs.rs#244)```
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)We can also iterate over [`Captures`] values instead of [`Match`] values, and
[247](https://docs.rs#247)that in turn permits accessing each component of the date via capturing groups:
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)```rust
[250](https://docs.rs#250)use regex_lite::Regex;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)let re = Regex::new(r"(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})").unwrap();
[253](https://docs.rs#253)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[254](https://docs.rs#254)// 'm' is a 'Match', and 'as_str()' returns the matching part of the haystack.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)let dates: Vec<(&str, &str, &str)> = re.captures_iter(hay).map(|caps| {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    // The unwraps are okay because every capture group must match if the whole
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    // regex matches, and in this context, we know we have a match.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    //
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    // Note that we use `caps.name("y").unwrap().as_str()` instead of
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    // `&caps["y"]` because the lifetime of the former is the same as the
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    // lifetime of `hay` above, but the lifetime of the latter is tied to the
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    // lifetime of `caps` due to how the `Index` trait is defined.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    let year = caps.name("y").unwrap().as_str();
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    let month = caps.name("m").unwrap().as_str();
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    let day = caps.name("d").unwrap().as_str();
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    (year, month, day)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)}).collect();
[268](https://docs.rs#268)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    ("1865", "04", "14"),
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ("1881", "07", "02"),
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    ("1901", "09", "06"),
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ("1963", "11", "22"),
[273](https://docs.rs#273)]);
[274](https://docs.rs#274)```
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)### Example: simpler capture group extraction
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)One can use [`Captures::extract`] to make the code from the previous example a
[279](https://docs.rs#279)bit simpler in this case:
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)```rust
[282](https://docs.rs#282)use regex_lite::Regex;
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)let re = Regex::new(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})").unwrap();
[285](https://docs.rs#285)let hay = "What do 1865-04-14, 1881-07-02, 1901-09-06 and 1963-11-22 have in common?";
[286](https://docs.rs#286)let dates: Vec<(&str, &str, &str)> = re.captures_iter(hay).map(|caps| {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    let (_, [year, month, day]) = caps.extract();
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    (year, month, day)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)}).collect();
[290](https://docs.rs#290)assert_eq!(dates, vec![
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ("1865", "04", "14"),
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    ("1881", "07", "02"),
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ("1901", "09", "06"),
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    ("1963", "11", "22"),
[295](https://docs.rs#295)]);
[296](https://docs.rs#296)```
[297](https://docs.rs#297)
[298](https://docs.rs#298)`Captures::extract` works by ensuring that the number of matching groups match
[299](https://docs.rs#299)the number of groups requested via the `[year, month, day]` syntax. If they do,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)then the substrings for each corresponding capture group are automatically
[301](https://docs.rs#301)returned in an appropriately sized array. Rust's syntax for pattern matching
[302](https://docs.rs#302)arrays does the rest.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)### Example: replacement with named capture groups
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)Building on the previous example, perhaps we'd like to rearrange the date
[307](https://docs.rs#307)formats. This can be done by finding each match and replacing it with
[308](https://docs.rs#308)something different. The [`Regex::replace_all`] routine provides a convenient
[309](https://docs.rs#309)way to do this, including by supporting references to named groups in the
[310](https://docs.rs#310)replacement string:
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)```rust
[313](https://docs.rs#313)use regex_lite::Regex;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)let re = Regex::new(r"(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})").unwrap();
[316](https://docs.rs#316)let before = "1973-01-05, 1975-08-25 and 1980-10-18";
[317](https://docs.rs#317)let after = re.replace_all(before, "$m/$d/$y");
[318](https://docs.rs#318)assert_eq!(after, "01/05/1973, 08/25/1975 and 10/18/1980");
[319](https://docs.rs#319)```
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)The replace methods are actually polymorphic in the replacement, which
[322](https://docs.rs#322)provides more flexibility than is seen here. (See the documentation for
[323](https://docs.rs#323)[`Regex::replace`] for more details.)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)### Example: verbose mode
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)When your regex gets complicated, you might consider using something other
[328](https://docs.rs#328)than regex. But if you stick with regex, you can use the `x` flag to enable
[329](https://docs.rs#329)insignificant whitespace mode or "verbose mode." In this mode, whitespace
[330](https://docs.rs#330)is treated as insignificant and one may write comments. This may make your
[331](https://docs.rs#331)patterns easier to comprehend.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)```rust
[334](https://docs.rs#334)use regex_lite::Regex;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)let re = Regex::new(r"(?x)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)  (?P<y>\d{4}) # the year
[338](https://docs.rs#338)  -
[339](https://docs.rs#339)  (?P<m>\d{2}) # the month
[340](https://docs.rs#340)  -
[341](https://docs.rs#341)  (?P<d>\d{2}) # the day
[342](https://docs.rs#342)").unwrap();
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)let before = "1973-01-05, 1975-08-25 and 1980-10-18";
[345](https://docs.rs#345)let after = re.replace_all(before, "$m/$d/$y");
[346](https://docs.rs#346)assert_eq!(after, "01/05/1973, 08/25/1975 and 10/18/1980");
[347](https://docs.rs#347)```
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)If you wish to match against whitespace in this mode, you can still use `\s`,
[350](https://docs.rs#350)`\n`, `\t`, etc. For escaping a single space character, you can escape it
[351](https://docs.rs#351)directly with `\ `, use its hex character code `\x20` or temporarily disable
[352](https://docs.rs#352)the `x` flag, e.g., `(?-x: )`.
[353](https://docs.rs#353)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)# Differences with the `regex` crate
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)As mentioned in the introduction above, the purpose of this crate is to
[357](https://docs.rs#357)prioritize small binary sizes and shorter Rust compilation times as much as
[358](https://docs.rs#358)possible. Namely, while the `regex` crate tends to eschew both binary size
[359](https://docs.rs#359)and compilation time in favor of faster searches and features, the
[360](https://docs.rs#360)`regex-lite` crate gives up faster searches and some functionality in exchange
[361](https://docs.rs#361)for smaller binary sizes and faster compilation times.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)The precise set of differences at the syntax level:
[364](https://docs.rs#364)
[365](https://docs.rs#365)* The Perl character classes are limited to ASCII codepoints. That is,
[366](https://docs.rs#366)`\d` is `[0-9]`, `\s` is `[\t\n\v\f\r ]` and `\w` is `[0-9A-Za-z_]`.
[367](https://docs.rs#367)* Unicode character classes of the form `\p{...}` and `\P{...}` are not
[368](https://docs.rs#368)supported at all. Note though that things like `[^β]` are still supported and
[369](https://docs.rs#369)will match any Unicode scalar value except for `β`.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)* Case insensitive searching is limited to ASCII case insensitivity.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)* Character class set operations other than union are not supported. That is,
[372](https://docs.rs#372)difference (`--`), intersection (`&&`) and symmetric difference (`~~`) are
[373](https://docs.rs#373)not available. These tend to be most useful with Unicode classes, which also
[374](https://docs.rs#374)aren't available.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)* Opt-in octal support is not available in this crate.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)And now at the API level:
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)* Currently, this crate only supports searching `&str`. It does not have APIs
[380](https://docs.rs#380)for searching `&[u8]` haystacks, although it is planned to add these in the
[381](https://docs.rs#381)future if there's demand.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)* There is no `RegexSet` in this crate and there are no plans to add it.
[383](https://docs.rs#383)* The `Error` type in this crate is completely opaque.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)Other than these things, the `regex-lite` crate is intended to be a drop-in
[386](https://docs.rs#386)replacement for the `regex` crate. In most cases, you can just replace `use
[387](https://docs.rs#387)regex::Regex;` with `use regex_lite::Regex;` and everything will work. (Unless
[388](https://docs.rs#388)you're depending on Unicode support in your regexes.)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)# Syntax
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)The syntax supported in this crate is documented below.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)
[394](https://docs.rs#394)### Matching one character
[395](https://docs.rs#395)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)<pre class="rust">
[397](https://docs.rs#397).             any character except new line (includes new line with s flag)
[398](https://docs.rs#398)[0-9]         any ASCII digit
[399](https://docs.rs#399)\d            digit ([0-9])
[400](https://docs.rs#400)\D            not digit
[401](https://docs.rs#401)</pre>
[402](https://docs.rs#402)
[403](https://docs.rs#403)### Character classes
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)<pre class="rust">
[406](https://docs.rs#406)[xyz]         A character class matching either x, y or z (union).
[407](https://docs.rs#407)[^xyz]        A character class matching any character except x, y and z.
[408](https://docs.rs#408)[a-z]         A character class matching any character in range a-z.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)[[:alpha:]]   ASCII character class ([A-Za-z])
[410](https://docs.rs#410)[[:^alpha:]]  Negated ASCII character class ([^A-Za-z])
[411](https://docs.rs#411)[\[\]]        Escaping in character classes (matching [ or ])
[412](https://docs.rs#412)</pre>
[413](https://docs.rs#413)
[414](https://docs.rs#414)Any ASCII or Perl character class may appear inside a bracketed `[...]` character
[415](https://docs.rs#415)class. For example, `[\s[:digit:]]` matches any digit or space character.
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)Precedence in character classes, from most binding to least:
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)1. Ranges: `[a-cd]` == `[[a-c]d]`
[420](https://docs.rs#420)2. Union: `[ab&&bc]` == `[[ab]&&[bc]]`
[421](https://docs.rs#421)3. Negation: `[^a-z&&b]` == `[^[a-z&&b]]`.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)
[423](https://docs.rs#423)### Composites
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)<pre class="rust">
[426](https://docs.rs#426)xy    concatenation (x followed by y)
[427](https://docs.rs#427)x|y   alternation (x or y, prefer x)
[428](https://docs.rs#428)</pre>
[429](https://docs.rs#429)
[430](https://docs.rs#430)This example shows how an alternation works, and what it means to prefer a
[431](https://docs.rs#431)branch in the alternation over subsequent branches.
[432](https://docs.rs#432)
[433](https://docs.rs#433)```
[434](https://docs.rs#434)use regex_lite::Regex;
[435](https://docs.rs#435)
[436](https://docs.rs#436)let haystack = "samwise";
[437](https://docs.rs#437)// If 'samwise' comes first in our alternation, then it is
[438](https://docs.rs#438)// preferred as a match, even if the regex engine could
[439](https://docs.rs#439)// technically detect that 'sam' led to a match earlier.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)let re = Regex::new(r"samwise|sam").unwrap();
[441](https://docs.rs#441)assert_eq!("samwise", re.find(haystack).unwrap().as_str());
[442](https://docs.rs#442)// But if 'sam' comes first, then it will match instead.
[443](https://docs.rs#443)// In this case, it is impossible for 'samwise' to match
[444](https://docs.rs#444)// because 'sam' is a prefix of it.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)let re = Regex::new(r"sam|samwise").unwrap();
[446](https://docs.rs#446)assert_eq!("sam", re.find(haystack).unwrap().as_str());
[447](https://docs.rs#447)```
[448](https://docs.rs#448)
[449](https://docs.rs#449)### Repetitions
[450](https://docs.rs#450)
[451](https://docs.rs#451)<pre class="rust">
[452](https://docs.rs#452)x*        zero or more of x (greedy)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)x+        one or more of x (greedy)
[454](https://docs.rs#454)x?        zero or one of x (greedy)
[455](https://docs.rs#455)x*?       zero or more of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[456](https://docs.rs#456)x+?       one or more of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[457](https://docs.rs#457)x??       zero or one of x (ungreedy/lazy)
[458](https://docs.rs#458)x{n,m}    at least n x and at most m x (greedy)
[459](https://docs.rs#459)x{n,}     at least n x (greedy)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)x{n}      exactly n x
[461](https://docs.rs#461)x{n,m}?   at least n x and at most m x (ungreedy/lazy)
[462](https://docs.rs#462)x{n,}?    at least n x (ungreedy/lazy)
[463](https://docs.rs#463)x{n}?     exactly n x
[464](https://docs.rs#464)</pre>
[465](https://docs.rs#465)
[466](https://docs.rs#466)### Empty matches
[467](https://docs.rs#467)
[468](https://docs.rs#468)<pre class="rust">
[469](https://docs.rs#469)^               the beginning of a haystack (or start-of-line with multi-line mode)
[470](https://docs.rs#470)$               the end of a haystack (or end-of-line with multi-line mode)
[471](https://docs.rs#471)\A              only the beginning of a haystack (even with multi-line mode enabled)
[472](https://docs.rs#472)\z              only the end of a haystack (even with multi-line mode enabled)
[473](https://docs.rs#473)\b              an ASCII word boundary (\w on one side and \W, \A, or \z on other)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)\B              not an ASCII word boundary
[475](https://docs.rs#475)\b{start}, \<   an ASCII start-of-word boundary (\W|\A on the left, \w on the right)
[476](https://docs.rs#476)\b{end}, \>     an ASCII end-of-word boundary (\w on the left, \W|\z on the right))
[477](https://docs.rs#477)\b{start-half}  half of an ASCII start-of-word boundary (\W|\A on the left)
[478](https://docs.rs#478)\b{end-half}    half of an ASCII end-of-word boundary (\W|\z on the right)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)</pre>
[480](https://docs.rs#480)
[481](https://docs.rs#481)The empty regex is valid and matches the empty string. For example, the
[482](https://docs.rs#482)empty regex matches `abc` at positions `0`, `1`, `2` and `3`. When using the
[483](https://docs.rs#483)top-level [`Regex`] on `&str` haystacks, an empty match that splits a codepoint
[484](https://docs.rs#484)is guaranteed to never be returned. For example:
[485](https://docs.rs#485)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)```rust
[487](https://docs.rs#487)let re = regex_lite::Regex::new(r"").unwrap();
[488](https://docs.rs#488)let ranges: Vec<_> = re.find_iter("💩").map(|m| m.range()).collect();
[489](https://docs.rs#489)assert_eq!(ranges, vec![0..0, 4..4]);
[490](https://docs.rs#490)```
[491](https://docs.rs#491)
[492](https://docs.rs#492)Note that an empty regex is distinct from a regex that can never match. For
[493](https://docs.rs#493)example, the regex `[^\s\S]` is a character class that represents the negation
[494](https://docs.rs#494)of `[\s\S]`, where the union of `\s` and `\S` corresponds to all Unicode scalar
[495](https://docs.rs#495)values. The negation of everything is nothing, which means the character class
[496](https://docs.rs#496)is empty. Since nothing is in the empty set, `[^\s\S]` matches nothing, not
[497](https://docs.rs#497)even the empty string.
[498](https://docs.rs#498)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)### Grouping and flags
[500](https://docs.rs#500)
[501](https://docs.rs#501)<pre class="rust">
[502](https://docs.rs#502)(exp)          numbered capture group (indexed by opening parenthesis)
[503](https://docs.rs#503)(?P<name>exp)  named (also numbered) capture group (names must be alpha-numeric)
[504](https://docs.rs#504)(?<name>exp)   named (also numbered) capture group (names must be alpha-numeric)
[505](https://docs.rs#505)(?:exp)        non-capturing group
[506](https://docs.rs#506)(?flags)       set flags within current group
[507](https://docs.rs#507)(?flags:exp)   set flags for exp (non-capturing)
[508](https://docs.rs#508)</pre>
[509](https://docs.rs#509)
[510](https://docs.rs#510)Capture group names must be any sequence of alpha-numeric Unicode codepoints,
[511](https://docs.rs#511)in addition to `.`, `_`, `[` and `]`. Names must start with either an `_` or
[512](https://docs.rs#512)an alphabetic codepoint. Alphabetic codepoints correspond to the `Alphabetic`
[513](https://docs.rs#513)Unicode property, while numeric codepoints correspond to the union of the
[514](https://docs.rs#514)`Decimal_Number`, `Letter_Number` and `Other_Number` general categories.
[515](https://docs.rs#515)
[516](https://docs.rs#516)Flags are each a single character. For example, `(?x)` sets the flag `x`
[517](https://docs.rs#517)and `(?-x)` clears the flag `x`. Multiple flags can be set or cleared at
[518](https://docs.rs#518)the same time: `(?xy)` sets both the `x` and `y` flags and `(?x-y)` sets
[519](https://docs.rs#519)the `x` flag and clears the `y` flag.
[520](https://docs.rs#520)
[521](https://docs.rs#521)All flags are by default disabled unless stated otherwise. They are:
[522](https://docs.rs#522)
[523](https://docs.rs#523)<pre class="rust">
[524](https://docs.rs#524)i     case-insensitive: letters match both upper and lower case
[525](https://docs.rs#525)m     multi-line mode: ^ and $ match begin/end of line
[526](https://docs.rs#526)s     allow . to match \n
[527](https://docs.rs#527)R     enables CRLF mode: when multi-line mode is enabled, \r\n is used
[528](https://docs.rs#528)U     swap the meaning of x* and x*?
[529](https://docs.rs#529)x     verbose mode, ignores whitespace and allow line comments (starting with `#`)
[530](https://docs.rs#530)</pre>
[531](https://docs.rs#531)
[532](https://docs.rs#532)Note that in verbose mode, whitespace is ignored everywhere, including within
[533](https://docs.rs#533)character classes. To insert whitespace, use its escaped form or a hex literal.
[534](https://docs.rs#534)For example, `\ ` or `\x20` for an ASCII space.
[535](https://docs.rs#535)
[536](https://docs.rs#536)Flags can be toggled within a pattern. Here's an example that matches
[537](https://docs.rs#537)case-insensitively for the first part but case-sensitively for the second part:
[538](https://docs.rs#538)
[539](https://docs.rs#539)```rust
[540](https://docs.rs#540)use regex_lite::Regex;
[541](https://docs.rs#541)
[542](https://docs.rs#542)let re = Regex::new(r"(?i)a+(?-i)b+").unwrap();
[543](https://docs.rs#543)let m = re.find("AaAaAbbBBBb").unwrap();
[544](https://docs.rs#544)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "AaAaAbb");
[545](https://docs.rs#545)```
[546](https://docs.rs#546)
[547](https://docs.rs#547)Notice that the `a+` matches either `a` or `A`, but the `b+` only matches
[548](https://docs.rs#548)`b`.
[549](https://docs.rs#549)
[550](https://docs.rs#550)Multi-line mode means `^` and `$` no longer match just at the beginning/end of
[551](https://docs.rs#551)the input, but also at the beginning/end of lines:
[552](https://docs.rs#552)
[553](https://docs.rs#553)```
[554](https://docs.rs#554)use regex_lite::Regex;
[555](https://docs.rs#555)
[556](https://docs.rs#556)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^line \d+").unwrap();
[557](https://docs.rs#557)let m = re.find("line one\nline 2\n").unwrap();
[558](https://docs.rs#558)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "line 2");
[559](https://docs.rs#559)```
[560](https://docs.rs#560)
[561](https://docs.rs#561)Note that `^` matches after new lines, even at the end of input:
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)```
[564](https://docs.rs#564)use regex_lite::Regex;
[565](https://docs.rs#565)
[566](https://docs.rs#566)let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^").unwrap();
[567](https://docs.rs#567)let m = re.find_iter("test\n").last().unwrap();
[568](https://docs.rs#568)assert_eq!((m.start(), m.end()), (5, 5));
[569](https://docs.rs#569)```
[570](https://docs.rs#570)
[571](https://docs.rs#571)When both CRLF mode and multi-line mode are enabled, then `^` and `$` will
[572](https://docs.rs#572)match either `\r` or `\n`, but never in the middle of a `\r\n`:
[573](https://docs.rs#573)
[574](https://docs.rs#574)```
[575](https://docs.rs#575)use regex_lite::Regex;
[576](https://docs.rs#576)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)let re = Regex::new(r"(?mR)^foo$").unwrap();
[578](https://docs.rs#578)let m = re.find("\r\nfoo\r\n").unwrap();
[579](https://docs.rs#579)assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "foo");
[580](https://docs.rs#580)```
[581](https://docs.rs#581)
[582](https://docs.rs#582)### Escape sequences
[583](https://docs.rs#583)
[584](https://docs.rs#584)Note that this includes all possible escape sequences, even ones that are
[585](https://docs.rs#585)documented elsewhere.
[586](https://docs.rs#586)
[587](https://docs.rs#587)<pre class="rust">
[588](https://docs.rs#588)\*              literal *, applies to all ASCII except [0-9A-Za-z<>]
[589](https://docs.rs#589)\a              bell (\x07)
[590](https://docs.rs#590)\f              form feed (\x0C)
[591](https://docs.rs#591)\t              horizontal tab
[592](https://docs.rs#592)\n              new line
[593](https://docs.rs#593)\r              carriage return
[594](https://docs.rs#594)\v              vertical tab (\x0B)
[595](https://docs.rs#595)\A              matches at the beginning of a haystack
[596](https://docs.rs#596)\z              matches at the end of a haystack
[597](https://docs.rs#597)\b              word boundary assertion
[598](https://docs.rs#598)\B              negated word boundary assertion
[599](https://docs.rs#599)\b{start}, \<   start-of-word boundary assertion
[600](https://docs.rs#600)\b{end}, \>     end-of-word boundary assertion
[601](https://docs.rs#601)\b{start-half}  half of a start-of-word boundary assertion
[602](https://docs.rs#602)\b{end-half}    half of a end-of-word boundary assertion
[603](https://docs.rs#603)\x7F            hex character code (exactly two digits)
[604](https://docs.rs#604)\x{10FFFF}      any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[605](https://docs.rs#605)\u007F          hex character code (exactly four digits)
[606](https://docs.rs#606)\u{7F}          any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[607](https://docs.rs#607)\U0000007F      hex character code (exactly eight digits)
[608](https://docs.rs#608)\U{7F}          any hex character code corresponding to a Unicode code point
[609](https://docs.rs#609)\d, \s, \w      Perl character class
[610](https://docs.rs#610)\D, \S, \W      negated Perl character class
[611](https://docs.rs#611)</pre>
[612](https://docs.rs#612)
[613](https://docs.rs#613)### Perl character classes (ASCII only)
[614](https://docs.rs#614)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)These character classes are short-hands for common groups of characters. In
[616](https://docs.rs#616)this crate, `\d`, `\s` and `\w` only consist of ASCII codepoints.
[617](https://docs.rs#617)
[618](https://docs.rs#618)<pre class="rust">

[624](https://docs.rs#624)\W     not word character
[625](https://docs.rs#625)</pre>

[649](https://docs.rs#649)
[650](https://docs.rs#650)# Untrusted input
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)This crate is meant to be able to run regex searches on untrusted haystacks
[653](https://docs.rs#653)without fear of [ReDoS]. This crate also, to a certain extent, supports
[654](https://docs.rs#654)untrusted patterns.
[655](https://docs.rs#655)
[656](https://docs.rs#656)[ReDoS]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ReDoS
[657](https://docs.rs#657)
[658](https://docs.rs#658)This crate differs from most (but not all) other regex engines in that it
[659](https://docs.rs#659)doesn't use unbounded backtracking to run a regex search. In those cases,
[660](https://docs.rs#660)one generally cannot use untrusted patterns *or* untrusted haystacks because
[661](https://docs.rs#661)it can be very difficult to know whether a particular pattern will result in
[662](https://docs.rs#662)catastrophic backtracking or not.
[663](https://docs.rs#663)
[664](https://docs.rs#664)We'll first discuss how this crate deals with untrusted inputs and then wrap
[665](https://docs.rs#665)it up with a realistic discussion about what practice really looks like.
[666](https://docs.rs#666)
[667](https://docs.rs#667)### Panics
[668](https://docs.rs#668)
[669](https://docs.rs#669)Outside of clearly documented cases, most APIs in this crate are intended to
[670](https://docs.rs#670)never panic regardless of the inputs given to them. For example, `Regex::new`,
[671](https://docs.rs#671)`Regex::is_match`, `Regex::find` and `Regex::captures` should never panic. That
[672](https://docs.rs#672)is, it is an API promise that those APIs will never panic no matter what inputs
[673](https://docs.rs#673)are given to them. With that said, regex engines are complicated beasts, and
[674](https://docs.rs#674)providing a rock solid guarantee that these APIs literally never panic is
[675](https://docs.rs#675)essentially equivalent to saying, "there are no bugs in this library." That is
[676](https://docs.rs#676)a bold claim, and not really one that can be feasibly made with a straight
[677](https://docs.rs#677)face.
[678](https://docs.rs#678)
[679](https://docs.rs#679)Don't get the wrong impression here. This crate is extensively tested, not just
[680](https://docs.rs#680)with unit and integration tests, but also via fuzz testing. For example, this
[681](https://docs.rs#681)crate is part of the [OSS-fuzz project]. Panics should be incredibly rare, but
[682](https://docs.rs#682)it is possible for bugs to exist, and thus possible for a panic to occur. If
[683](https://docs.rs#683)you need a rock solid guarantee against panics, then you should wrap calls into
[684](https://docs.rs#684)this library with [`std::panic::catch_unwind`].
[685](https://docs.rs#685)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)It's also worth pointing out that this library will generally panic when other
[687](https://docs.rs#687)regex engines would commit undefined behavior. When undefined behavior occurs,
[688](https://docs.rs#688)your program might continue as if nothing bad has happened, but it also might
[689](https://docs.rs#689)mean your program is open to the worst kinds of exploits. In contrast, the
[690](https://docs.rs#690)worst thing a panic can do is a denial of service.
[691](https://docs.rs#691)
[692](https://docs.rs#692)[OSS-fuzz project]: https://android.googlesource.com/platform/external/oss-fuzz/+/refs/tags/android-t-preview-1/projects/rust-regex/
[693](https://docs.rs#693)[`std::panic::catch_unwind`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/panic/fn.catch_unwind.html
[694](https://docs.rs#694)
[695](https://docs.rs#695)### Untrusted patterns
[696](https://docs.rs#696)
[697](https://docs.rs#697)The principal way this crate deals with them is by limiting their size by
[698](https://docs.rs#698)default. The size limit can be configured via [`RegexBuilder::size_limit`]. The
[699](https://docs.rs#699)idea of a size limit is that compiling a pattern into a `Regex` will fail if it
[700](https://docs.rs#700)becomes "too big." Namely, while *most* resources consumed by compiling a regex
[701](https://docs.rs#701)are approximately proportional to the length of the pattern itself, there is
[702](https://docs.rs#702)one particular exception to this: counted repetitions. Namely, this pattern:
[703](https://docs.rs#703)
[704](https://docs.rs#704)```text
[705](https://docs.rs#705)a{5}{5}{5}{5}{5}{5}
[706](https://docs.rs#706)```
[707](https://docs.rs#707)
[708](https://docs.rs#708)Is equivalent to this pattern:
[709](https://docs.rs#709)
[710](https://docs.rs#710)```text
[711](https://docs.rs#711)a{15625}
[712](https://docs.rs#712)```
[713](https://docs.rs#713)
[714](https://docs.rs#714)In both of these cases, the actual pattern string is quite small, but the
[715](https://docs.rs#715)resulting `Regex` value is quite large. Indeed, as the first pattern shows,
[716](https://docs.rs#716)it isn't enough to locally limit the size of each repetition because they can
[717](https://docs.rs#717)be stacked in a way that results in exponential growth.
[718](https://docs.rs#718)
[719](https://docs.rs#719)To provide a bit more context, a simplified view of regex compilation looks
[720](https://docs.rs#720)like this:
[721](https://docs.rs#721)
[722](https://docs.rs#722)* The pattern string is parsed into a structured representation called an HIR
[723](https://docs.rs#723)(high-level intermediate representation). Counted repetitions are not expanded
[724](https://docs.rs#724)in this stage. That is, the size of the HIR is proportional to the size
[725](https://docs.rs#725)of the pattern with "reasonable" constant factors. In other words, one can
[726](https://docs.rs#726)reasonably limit the memory used by an HIR by limiting the length of the
[727](https://docs.rs#727)pattern string.
[728](https://docs.rs#728)* The HIR is compiled into a [Thompson NFA]. This is the stage at which
[729](https://docs.rs#729)something like `\w{5}` is rewritten to `\w\w\w\w\w`. Thus, this is the stage
[730](https://docs.rs#730)at which [`RegexBuilder::size_limit`] is enforced. If the NFA exceeds the
[731](https://docs.rs#731)configured size, then this stage will fail.
[732](https://docs.rs#732)
[733](https://docs.rs#733)[Thompson NFA]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thompson%27s_construction
[734](https://docs.rs#734)
[735](https://docs.rs#735)The size limit helps avoid two different kinds of exorbitant resource usage:
[736](https://docs.rs#736)
[737](https://docs.rs#737)* It avoids permitting exponential memory usage based on the size of the
[738](https://docs.rs#738)pattern string.
[739](https://docs.rs#739)* It avoids long search times. This will be discussed in more detail in the
[740](https://docs.rs#740)next section, but worst case search time *is* dependent on the size of the
[741](https://docs.rs#741)regex. So keeping regexes limited to a reasonable size is also a way of keeping
[742](https://docs.rs#742)search times reasonable.
[743](https://docs.rs#743)
[744](https://docs.rs#744)Finally, it's worth pointing out that regex compilation is guaranteed to take
[745](https://docs.rs#745)worst case `O(m)` time, where `m` is proportional to the size of regex. The
[746](https://docs.rs#746)size of the regex here is *after* the counted repetitions have been expanded.
[747](https://docs.rs#747)
[748](https://docs.rs#748)**Advice for those using untrusted regexes**: limit the pattern length to
[749](https://docs.rs#749)something small and expand it as needed. Configure [`RegexBuilder::size_limit`]
[750](https://docs.rs#750)to something small and then expand it as needed.
[751](https://docs.rs#751)
[752](https://docs.rs#752)### Untrusted haystacks
[753](https://docs.rs#753)
[754](https://docs.rs#754)The main way this crate guards against searches from taking a long time is by
[755](https://docs.rs#755)using algorithms that guarantee a `O(m * n)` worst case time and space bound.
[756](https://docs.rs#756)Namely:
[757](https://docs.rs#757)
[758](https://docs.rs#758)* `m` is proportional to the size of the regex, where the size of the regex
[759](https://docs.rs#759)includes the expansion of all counted repetitions. (See the previous section on
[760](https://docs.rs#760)untrusted patterns.)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)* `n` is proportional to the length, in bytes, of the haystack.
[762](https://docs.rs#762)
[763](https://docs.rs#763)In other words, if you consider `m` to be a constant (for example, the regex
[764](https://docs.rs#764)pattern is a literal in the source code), then the search can be said to run
[765](https://docs.rs#765)in "linear time." Or equivalently, "linear time with respect to the size of the
[766](https://docs.rs#766)haystack."
[767](https://docs.rs#767)
[768](https://docs.rs#768)But the `m` factor here is important not to ignore. If a regex is
[769](https://docs.rs#769)particularly big, the search times can get quite slow. This is why, in part,
[770](https://docs.rs#770)[`RegexBuilder::size_limit`] exists.
[771](https://docs.rs#771)
[772](https://docs.rs#772)**Advice for those searching untrusted haystacks**: As long as your regexes
[773](https://docs.rs#773)are not enormous, you should expect to be able to search untrusted haystacks
[774](https://docs.rs#774)without fear. If you aren't sure, you should benchmark it. Unlike backtracking
[775](https://docs.rs#775)engines, if your regex is so big that it's likely to result in slow searches,
[776](https://docs.rs#776)this is probably something you'll be able to observe regardless of what the
[777](https://docs.rs#777)haystack is made up of.
[778](https://docs.rs#778)
[779](https://docs.rs#779)### Iterating over matches
[780](https://docs.rs#780)
[781](https://docs.rs#781)One thing that is perhaps easy to miss is that the worst case time
[782](https://docs.rs#782)complexity bound of `O(m * n)` applies to methods like [`Regex::is_match`],
[783](https://docs.rs#783)[`Regex::find`] and [`Regex::captures`]. It does **not** apply to
[784](https://docs.rs#784)[`Regex::find_iter`] or [`Regex::captures_iter`]. Namely, since iterating over
[785](https://docs.rs#785)all matches can execute many searches, and each search can scan the entire
[786](https://docs.rs#786)haystack, the worst case time complexity for iterators is `O(m * n^2)`.
[787](https://docs.rs#787)
[788](https://docs.rs#788)One example of where this occurs is when a pattern consists of an alternation,
[789](https://docs.rs#789)where an earlier branch of the alternation requires scanning the entire
[790](https://docs.rs#790)haystack only to discover that there is no match. It also requires a later
[791](https://docs.rs#791)branch of the alternation to have matched at the beginning of the search. For
[792](https://docs.rs#792)example, consider the pattern `.*[^A-Z]|[A-Z]` and the haystack `AAAAA`. The
[793](https://docs.rs#793)first search will scan to the end looking for matches of `.*[^A-Z]` even though
[794](https://docs.rs#794)a finite automata engine (as in this crate) knows that `[A-Z]` has already
[795](https://docs.rs#795)matched the first character of the haystack. This is due to the greedy nature
[796](https://docs.rs#796)of regex searching. That first search will report a match at the first `A` only
[797](https://docs.rs#797)after scanning to the end to discover that no other match exists. The next
[798](https://docs.rs#798)search then begins at the second `A` and the behavior repeats.
[799](https://docs.rs#799)
[800](https://docs.rs#800)There is no way to avoid this. This means that if both patterns and haystacks
[801](https://docs.rs#801)are untrusted and you're iterating over all matches, you're susceptible
[802](https://docs.rs#802)to worst case quadratic time complexity. One possible way to mitigate
[803](https://docs.rs#803)this is to switch to the lower level `regex-automata` crate and use its
[804](https://docs.rs#804)`meta::Regex` iterator APIs. There, you can configure the search to operate
[805](https://docs.rs#805)in "earliest" mode by passing a `Input::new(haystack).earliest(true)` to
[806](https://docs.rs#806)`meta::Regex::find_iter` (for example). By enabling this mode, you give up
[807](https://docs.rs#807)the normal greedy match semantics of regex searches and instead ask the regex
[808](https://docs.rs#808)engine to immediately stop as soon as a match has been found. Enabling this
[809](https://docs.rs#809)mode will thus restore the worst case `O(m * n)` time complexity bound, but at
[810](https://docs.rs#810)the cost of different semantics.
[811](https://docs.rs#811)
[812](https://docs.rs#812)### Untrusted inputs in practice
[813](https://docs.rs#813)
[814](https://docs.rs#814)While providing a `O(m * n)` worst case time bound on all searches goes a long
[815](https://docs.rs#815)way toward preventing [ReDoS], that doesn't mean every search you can possibly
[816](https://docs.rs#816)run will complete without burning CPU time. In general, there are a few ways
[817](https://docs.rs#817)for the `m * n` time bound to still bite you:
[818](https://docs.rs#818)
[819](https://docs.rs#819)* You are searching an exceptionally long haystack. No matter how you slice
[820](https://docs.rs#820)it, a longer haystack will take more time to search.
[821](https://docs.rs#821)* Very large regexes can searches to be quite slow due to increasing the size
[822](https://docs.rs#822)`m` in the worst case `O(m * n)` bound. This is especially true when they
[823](https://docs.rs#823)are combined with counted repetitions. While the regex size limit above will
[824](https://docs.rs#824)protect you from the most egregious cases, the default size limit still
[825](https://docs.rs#825)permits pretty big regexes that can execute more slowly than one might expect.
[826](https://docs.rs#826)* While routines like [`Regex::find`] and [`Regex::captures`] guarantee
[827](https://docs.rs#827)worst case `O(m * n)` search time, routines like [`Regex::find_iter`] and
[828](https://docs.rs#828)[`Regex::captures_iter`] actually have worst case `O(m * n^2)` search time.
[829](https://docs.rs#829)This is because `find_iter` runs many searches, and each search takes worst
[830](https://docs.rs#830)case `O(m * n)` time. Thus, iteration of all matches in a haystack has
[831](https://docs.rs#831)worst case `O(m * n^2)`. A good example of a pattern that exhibits this is
[832](https://docs.rs#832)`(?:A+){1000}|` or even `.*[^A-Z]|[A-Z]`.
[833](https://docs.rs#833)
[834](https://docs.rs#834)In general, untrusted haystacks are easier to stomach than untrusted patterns.
[835](https://docs.rs#835)Untrusted patterns give a lot more control to the caller to impact the
[836](https://docs.rs#836)performance of a search. Therefore, permitting untrusted patterns means that
[837](https://docs.rs#837)your only line of defense is to put a limit on how big `m` (and perhaps also
[838](https://docs.rs#838)`n`) can be in `O(m * n)`. `n` is limited by simply inspecting the length
[839](https://docs.rs#839)of the haystack while `m` is limited by *both* applying a limit to the
[840](https://docs.rs#840)length of the pattern *and* a limit on the compiled size of the regex via
[841](https://docs.rs#841)[`RegexBuilder::size_limit`].
[842](https://docs.rs#842)
[843](https://docs.rs#843)It bears repeating: if you're accepting untrusted patterns, it would be a good
[844](https://docs.rs#844)idea to start with conservative limits on `m` and `n`, and then carefully
[845](https://docs.rs#845)increase them as needed.
[846](https://docs.rs#846)*/
[847](https://docs.rs#847)

# Regex in regex_lite - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/regex-lite/0.1.9/regex_lite/struct.Regex.html

`pub struct Regex { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A compiled regular expression for searching Unicode haystacks.

A `Regex` can be used to search haystacks, split haystacks into substrings
or replace substrings in a haystack with a different substring. All
searching is done with an implicit `(?s:.)*?` at the beginning and end of
an pattern. To force an expression to match the whole string (or a prefix
or a suffix), you must use an anchor like `^` or `$` (or `\A` and `\z`).

While this crate will handle Unicode strings (whether in the regular
expression or in the haystack), all positions returned are **byte
offsets**. Every byte offset is guaranteed to be at a Unicode code point
boundary. That is, all offsets returned by the `Regex` API are guaranteed
to be ranges that can slice a `&str` without panicking.

The only methods that allocate new strings are the string replacement methods. All other methods (searching and splitting) return borrowed references into the haystack given.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Find the offsets of a US phone number:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new("[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}").unwrap();
let m = re.find("phone: 111-222-3333").unwrap();
assert_eq!(7..19, m.range());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-extracting-capture-groups)Example: extracting capture groups

A common way to use regexes is with capture groups. That is, instead of just looking for matches of an entire regex, parentheses are used to create groups that represent part of the match.

For example, consider a haystack with multiple lines, and each line has
three whitespace delimited fields where the second field is expected to be
a number and the third field a boolean. To make this convenient, we use
the [ Captures::extract](https://docs.rs/struct.Captures.html#method.extract) API to put the strings that match each group
into a fixed size array:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let hay = "
rabbit         54 true
groundhog 2 true
does not match
fox   109    false
";
let re = Regex::new(r"(?m)^\s*(\S+)\s+([0-9]+)\s+(true|false)\s*$").unwrap();
let mut fields: Vec<(&str, i64, bool)> = vec![];
for (_, [f1, f2, f3]) in re.captures_iter(hay).map(|caps| caps.extract()) {
    fields.push((f1, f2.parse()?, f3.parse()?));
}
assert_eq!(fields, vec![
    ("rabbit", 54, true),
    ("groundhog", 2, true),
    ("fox", 109, false),
]);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Compiles a regular expression. Once compiled, it can be used repeatedly to search, split or replace substrings in a haystack.

Note that regex compilation tends to be a somewhat expensive process, and unlike higher level environments, compilation is not automatically cached for you. One should endeavor to compile a regex once and then reuse it. For example, it’s a bad idea to compile the same regex repeatedly in a loop.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If an invalid pattern is given, then an error is returned.
An error is also returned if the pattern is valid, but would
produce a regex that is bigger than the configured size limit via
[ RegexBuilder::size_limit](https://docs.rs/struct.RegexBuilder.html#method.size_limit). (A reasonable size limit is enabled by
default.)

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
// An Invalid pattern because of an unclosed parenthesis
assert!(Regex::new(r"foo(bar").is_err());
// An invalid pattern because the regex would be too big
// because Unicode tends to inflate things.
assert!(Regex::new(r"\w{1000000}").is_err());
```
Returns true if and only if there is a match for the regex anywhere in the haystack given.

It is recommended to use this method if all you need to do is test whether a match exists, since the underlying matching engine may be able to do less work.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

Test if some haystack contains at least one word with exactly 13 word characters:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"\b\w{13}\b").unwrap();
let hay = "I categorically deny having triskaidekaphobia.";
assert!(re.is_match(hay));
```
This routine searches for the first match of this regex in the
haystack given, and if found, returns a [ Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html). The

`Match`
provides access to both the byte offsets of the match and the actual
substring that matched.Note that this should only be used if you want to find the entire
match. If instead you just want to test the existence of a match,
it’s potentially faster to use `Regex::is_match(hay)` instead of
`Regex::find(hay).is_some()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

Find the first word with exactly 13 word characters:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"\b\w{13}\b").unwrap();
let hay = "I categorically deny having triskaidekaphobia.";
let mat = re.find(hay).unwrap();
assert_eq!(2..15, mat.range());
assert_eq!("categorically", mat.as_str());
```
Returns an iterator that yields successive non-overlapping matches in
the given haystack. The iterator yields values of type [ Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#time-complexity)Time complexity

Note that since `find_iter` runs potentially many searches on the
haystack and since each search has worst case `O(m * n)` time
complexity, the overall worst case time complexity for iteration is
`O(m * n^2)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

Find every word with exactly 13 word characters:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"\b\w{13}\b").unwrap();
let hay = "Retroactively relinquishing remunerations is reprehensible.";
let matches: Vec<_> = re.find_iter(hay).map(|m| m.as_str()).collect();
assert_eq!(matches, vec![
    "Retroactively",
    "relinquishing",
    "remunerations",
    "reprehensible",
]);
```
This routine searches for the first match of this regex in the haystack
given, and if found, returns not only the overall match but also the
matches of each capture group in the regex. If no match is found, then
`None` is returned.

Capture group `0` always corresponds to an implicit unnamed group that
includes the entire match. If a match is found, this group is always
present. Subsequent groups may be named and are numbered, starting
at 1, by the order in which the opening parenthesis appears in the
pattern. For example, in the pattern `(?<a>.(?<b>.))(?<c>.)`, `a`,
`b` and `c` correspond to capture group indices `1`, `2` and `3`,
respectively.

You should only use `captures` if you need access to the capture group
matches. Otherwise, [ Regex::find](https://docs.rs/struct.Regex.html#method.find) is generally faster for discovering
just the overall match.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

Say you have some haystack with movie names and their release years, like “‘Citizen Kane’ (1941)”. It’d be nice if we could search for substrings looking like that, while also extracting the movie name and its release year separately. The example below shows how to do that.

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"'([^']+)'\s+\((\d{4})\)").unwrap();
let hay = "Not my favorite movie: 'Citizen Kane' (1941).";
let caps = re.captures(hay).unwrap();
assert_eq!(caps.get(0).unwrap().as_str(), "'Citizen Kane' (1941)");
assert_eq!(caps.get(1).unwrap().as_str(), "Citizen Kane");
assert_eq!(caps.get(2).unwrap().as_str(), "1941");
// You can also access the groups by index using the Index notation.
// Note that this will panic on an invalid index. In this case, these
// accesses are always correct because the overall regex will only
// match when these capture groups match.
assert_eq!(&caps[0], "'Citizen Kane' (1941)");
assert_eq!(&caps[1], "Citizen Kane");
assert_eq!(&caps[2], "1941");
```
Note that the full match is at capture group `0`. Each subsequent
capture group is indexed by the order of its opening `(`.

We can make this example a bit clearer by using *named* capture groups:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"'(?<title>[^']+)'\s+\((?<year>\d{4})\)").unwrap();
let hay = "Not my favorite movie: 'Citizen Kane' (1941).";
let caps = re.captures(hay).unwrap();
assert_eq!(caps.get(0).unwrap().as_str(), "'Citizen Kane' (1941)");
assert_eq!(caps.name("title").unwrap().as_str(), "Citizen Kane");
assert_eq!(caps.name("year").unwrap().as_str(), "1941");
// You can also access the groups by name using the Index notation.
// Note that this will panic on an invalid group name. In this case,
// these accesses are always correct because the overall regex will
// only match when these capture groups match.
assert_eq!(&caps[0], "'Citizen Kane' (1941)");
assert_eq!(&caps["title"], "Citizen Kane");
assert_eq!(&caps["year"], "1941");
```
Here we name the capture groups, which we can access with the `name`
method or the `Index` notation with a `&str`. Note that the named
capture groups are still accessible with `get` or the `Index` notation
with a `usize`.

The `0`th capture group is always unnamed, so it must always be
accessed with `get(0)` or `[0]`.

Finally, one other way to get the matched substrings is with the
[ Captures::extract](https://docs.rs/struct.Captures.html#method.extract) API:

```
use regex_lite::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"'([^']+)'\s+\((\d{4})\)").unwrap();
let hay = "Not my favorite movie: 'Citizen Kane' (1941).";
let (full, [title, year]) = re.captures(hay).unwrap().extract();
assert_eq!(full, "'Citizen Kane' (1941)");
assert_eq!(title, "Citizen Kane");
assert_eq!(year, "1941");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/regex_lite/string.rs.html#411-422)#### pub fn [captures_iter](https://docs.rs#method.captures_iter)<'r, 'h>(
    &'r self,
